exam: What bedside signs differentiate delirium tremens from simple alcohol withdrawal? — Presence of visual/tactile hallucinations, autonomic storm, and CIWA‑Ar >20.

A patient with chronic alcohol use presents with fever, tachycardia, and confusion 72 h after stopping drinking. What is your immediate management? — Start benzodiazepine titration, give thiamine, monitor vitals, and assess for infection.
Why is diazepam preferred over lorazepam in a low‑resource setting? — Diazepam is inexpensive, long‑acting, and available in oral/IV forms; it provides smoother control with fewer dose adjustments.
How would you rule out malaria as a cause of delirium in a Tanzanian hospital? — Perform rapid diagnostic test; if positive, treat malaria while continuing withdrawal management.
Explain why high‑dose haloperidol is avoided in DT. — It can prolong QT interval and lower seizure threshold, worsening autonomic instability.

A patient on DT develops a new rash and fever. What complication should you suspect and what test is needed? — Consider drug‑induced hypersensitivity or infection; obtain full blood count and blood cultures.
What long‑term strategy reduces recurrence of DT after discharge? — Enrol in alcohol cessation program, provide thiamine supplementation, and consider relapse‑prevention agents if available.
ai.title: Delirium Tremens
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Delirium tremens is a severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome with acute confusion, autonomic overactivity and hallucinations. Prompt recognition, supportive care and specific pharmacotherapy are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: DSM‑5 criteria: recent alcohol cessation, disturbance in attention/awareness, change in cognition, evidence of physiologic dependence, not better explained by another condition.
sections.p: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness and cognition occurring 48–96 h after abrupt cessation or reduction of heavy alcohol use, characterised by agitation, visual hallucinations and autonomic hyperactivity.

b: Mild: CIWA‑Ar ≤10 – outpatient observation.
Moderate: 11‑20 – ward level care.
Severe (DT): >20 – high‑dependency or ICU.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA‑Ar) score; >20 indicates severe withdrawal requiring intensive monitoring.

b: Chronic heavy alcohol use with sudden cessation.
Concurrent infections (TB, malaria, HIV opportunistic infections).
Electrolyte disturbances (hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia).
Use of sedative‑hypnotics or abrupt withdrawal of benzodiazepines.
sections.p: The primary cause is abrupt reduction of chronic alcohol intake. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing infections or metabolic disturbances can precipitate or worsen DT.

b: Tremor, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, fever.
Confusion, disorientation, fluctuating consciousness.
Visual hallucinations (e.g., insects), tactile hallucinations, persecutory ideas.
Seizures may precede or accompany DT.
sections.p: Patients develop a triad of autonomic hyperactivity, altered mental status and perceptual disturbances.
Targeted tests confirm withdrawal, rule out mimics and identify treatable complications.

t.b: Is hypoglycaemia contributing to altered mental status? Low → give dextrose.
Are electrolyte deficits present that increase seizure risk? Low Mg/K → replace.
Is infection present? Elevated WCC suggests infection; treat accordingly.
Is chronic alcohol use confirmed? Elevated GGT supports diagnosis.
Are other substances contributing? Positive result may alter management.

b: Sustained fever >38.5 °C – risk of aspiration pneumonia.
Refractory hypertension or tachyarrhythmia – cardiac ischemia.
Seizure clusters – status epilepticus.
Severe dehydration or electrolyte collapse.
sections.p: Uncontrolled autonomic storm and seizures can rapidly become fatal.

b: Fluid & electrolyte replacement: correct hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, and dehydration.
Antipsychotic (haloperidol) only for severe agitation unresponsive to benzodiazepine; avoid high doses due to QT prolongation.
Treat underlying infection or metabolic cause if identified.
sections.p: Treat the withdrawal, support vital functions and prevent complications. In low‑resource settings, use readily available benzodiazepines and monitor clinically.

b: Referral to counseling, community support groups, or pharmacologic relapse‑prevention (naltrexone, acamprosate) when available.
Schedule outpatient review within 1‑2 weeks to assess withdrawal sequelae and nutritional status.
Educate patient and family on gradual tapering if future cessation is needed.
sections.p: After resolution, arrange long‑term alcohol dependence treatment and monitor for relapse.

b: Alcohol‑induced psychotic disorder – persistent hallucinations without autonomic storm.
Acute delirium from infection (e.g., malaria, meningitis).
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome – rigidity, hyperthermia, elevated CK.
sections.p: Several acute neuro‑psychiatric states mimic DT.

b: Normal liver enzymes do not exclude chronic alcohol use; rely on GGT or clinical history.
Serum magnesium may be within reference range but intracellular depletion still exists – treat empirically if low risk.
sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite severe withdrawal.

whenToSeekHelp: Seizure lasting >5 min or recurrent seizures
